title: Three years quietly
hookLine: for about three years the call is private, person to person

cards: No speeches. No crowd gathered at the hill. For a long stretch at the beginning, the message in Mecca travels the way a family recipe travels: one person leans toward another and says, come, let me tell you something.
A friend to a friend. A brother to a sister. A master's household to a servant.
Ibn Ishaq, the early biographer, gives this quiet season a length. Today: Ibn Ishaq.

teach.b: Ibn Ishaq writes that three years passed between the time the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, kept his message private and the time he was commanded to make it public.
Some other writers count the time differently, so hold the number loosely; the shape is what the sirah keeps. First quietly, then openly. What did quiet look like?
The last few days of this path: Khadijah in the house, Ali and Zayd at the table, Abu Bakr bringing his friends one conversation at a time, prayer in the valleys, then behind al-Arqam's door.

teach.h: FACE TO FACE, ONE AT A TIME.
teach.b: People heard it from someone they already knew, face to face, with time for questions. Why begin that way? The sources don't give one reason, and readers offer several.
Some point to protection: a small group was easy to crush. Some point to teaching: the first believers needed time to learn the verses and pray together before anything was asked of them in public.
Some simply notice that this is how trust moves, from someone you know. Then the season ends.
The Qur'an gives a command that Pickthall translates: "So proclaim that which thou art commanded." And another verse tells him to warn his nearest kin.

teach.h: SO PROCLAIM THAT WHICH THOU ART COMMANDED.
teach.b: What he does with that command is tomorrow's story. Today is the quiet before it, and the quiet was not empty. It built the people who would stand beside him.

how: In sirah study Muslims divide the Meccan call into a private stage and a public stage, and the early private stage is often discussed as a model of patient, personal invitation.

practice: Recall a time someone told you something good one to one, a piece of advice, a line of scripture, a word of praise, and remember how it was said and what made it easy to hear.
Then choose one small good thing of your own you could pass on the same way, to one person, with no audience; if you pray, ask that it reach them well.
